common_misconceptions.misconception: Students use avoir for all verbs in the perfect tense, missing the MRS VANDERTRAMP/être verbs (aller, venir, arriver, partir, etc.) and reflexive verbs which take être.
common_misconceptions.source: Pearson Edexcel GCSE French 1FR1 Specification — Appendix 2 Grammar (perfect tense with être/avoir), qualifications.pearson.com

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students default adjectives to masculine singular even when the noun is feminine or plural (e.g. 'la maison est grand' instead of 'grande'). Gender of nouns is frequently misremembered (le/la confusion).
common_misconceptions.source: Pearson Edexcel GCSE French 1FR1 Specification — Appendix 2 Grammar (adjective agreement), qualifications.pearson.com

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students translate word-for-word, producing English word order in French (e.g. putting adjectives before most nouns, omitting the definite article where French requires it, e.g. 'J'aime musique' for 'I like music').
common_misconceptions.source: Pearson Edexcel GCSE French 1FR1 Paper 4 Writing — sentences requiring translation into French, qualifications.pearson.com/1FR1

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students transcribe French phonemes using English spelling intuition — missing silent final consonants, confusing nasal vowels (an/en, on/un), and writing 'é' for 'er/ez' endings.
common_misconceptions.source: Pearson Edexcel GCSE French 1FR1 Paper 2 Section B (Dictation, 10 marks), qualifications.pearson.com/1FR1

common_misconceptions.topic: Reflexive verbs in past and present
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students drop the reflexive pronoun or place it incorrectly (e.g. 'je lève' instead of 'je me lève'), and use avoir instead of être for the perfect tense of reflexives.
common_misconceptions.source: Pearson Edexcel GCSE French 1FR1 Specification — Appendix 2 Grammar (reflexive verbs), qualifications.pearson.com

common_misconceptions.topic: Definite article with abstract nouns and general statements
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students omit the definite article in contexts where French requires it (e.g. 'La santé est importante' not 'Santé est importante'; 'J'aime le sport' not 'J'aime sport').
common_misconceptions.source: Pearson Edexcel GCSE French 1FR1 Specification — Appendix 2 Grammar (determiners), qualifications.pearson.com

common_misconceptions.topic: Partitive articles with food and drink
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students use definite articles with food/drink quantities (e.g. 'je mange le pain') or drop the article entirely. They also forget that partitive articles become 'de' after negation and expressions of quantity.
common_misconceptions.source: Pearson Edexcel GCSE French 1FR1 Specification — Appendix 2 Grammar (partitive articles, de after negation), qualifications.pearson.com

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students prepare scripted answers and freeze when prompts deviate. Edexcel role-plays are always set in one of nine prescribed transactional settings (café/restaurant, shop, hotel, train station, tourist info, cinema/theatre, campsite, leisure centre, doctor's surgery, in town).
common_misconceptions.source: Pearson Edexcel GCSE French 1FR1 Paper 1 Speaking — role play (10 marks, transactional), qualifications.pearson.com/1FR1

student_errors_by_question_type.Dictation (Paper 2 Section B): Students lose marks by spelling French words phonetically using English conventions. Silent final consonants (-s, -t, -d, -x) and the é/er/ez ending cluster are frequent error hotspots. Source: Edexcel 1FR1 Paper 2 Section B is worth 10 marks at both Foundation and Higher tiers.
student_errors_by_question_type.Translation into English (Paper 3 Sectio: Students over-literal translate (e.g. 'J'ai faim' as 'I have hunger' instead of 'I am hungry') and miss the avoir + noun idioms. They also lose marks for key-message omissions when they skip a clause they don't understand. Source: Edexcel 1FR1 Paper 3 Section B Translation, 10 marks.
student_errors_by_question_type.Translation into French (Paper 4): Students produce English word order and forget gender agreement. They also under-use the perfect tense (defaulting to present) when English uses past tenses. Source: Edexcel 1FR1 Paper 4 Writing — translation task into French.
student_errors_by_question_type.Role-play (Paper 1 Task 2): Students hesitate at the unpredictable question, give one-word answers rather than full sentences, and over-rely on memorised scripts. The role-play is set in a prescribed transactional setting (café, hotel, train station, tourist info, etc.) — students must respond flexibly to prompts. Source: Edexcel 1FR1 Paper 1 Task 2 Role Play, 10 marks (Foundation and Higher).
student_errors_by_question_type.Picture card and conversation (Paper 1 T: Students describe only what they see (present tense observations) and fail to extend to past and future tenses or opinions, which are needed to access higher marks. Source: Edexcel 1FR1 Paper 1 Task 3 — picture description (12 marks) plus broader conversation (16 marks).
student_errors_by_question_type.Open writing tasks (Paper 4): Students write in one tense throughout, under-use connectives and subordinate clauses, and attempt complex structures outside their vocabulary. Tier-specific word counts reward range over ambition. Source: Edexcel 1FR1 Paper 4 Writing structure.

topic_weighting_notes: All four papers are equally weighted at 25%. Drilling should be balanced across skills — not weighted toward content knowledge.

Theme 1 (My personal world) and Theme 2 (Lifestyle and wellbeing) provide the richest vocabulary for the Writing and Speaking papers because students can draw on personal experience. Drill them early and revisit across all units.
Theme 6 (Travel and tourism) is the highest-yield theme for perfect tense practice since past-holiday narratives are a staple of writing prompts and picture cards.
Theme 4 (Media and technology) and Theme 3 (My neighbourhood) provide the strongest opportunity for opinion structures, comparatives and relative pronouns at Higher tier.
Sound-symbol correspondences are tested in both the Dictation section of Paper 2 and the Read Aloud task of Paper 1. They are a high-stakes area in the new specification.

Higher tier vocabulary adds an additional layer on top of Foundation — focus Higher-only problems on the additional grammar (passive voice, subjunctive after key conjunctions, ne…que, complex relative pronouns, regular future tense inflections) rather than just more words.
Equality (Theme 1) and mental wellbeing (Theme 2) are pitched at Higher tier in this plan because they require abstract opinion language and Higher-tier vocab.
current_spec_changes: First teaching September 2024, first exams 2026. The 1FR1 specification replaces the legacy Edexcel French GCSE.
Dictation is now a distinct section of Paper 2 (10 marks at both tiers). Source: Edexcel 1FR1 Paper 2 Section B.
Read Aloud is a new task in Paper 1 Speaking. Foundation 35–40 words in 5 sentences; Higher 50–55 words in 4 sentences. Source: Edexcel 1FR1 Paper 1 Task 1.
Vocabulary is prescribed in Appendix 1 of the specification at Foundation and Higher tiers; texts will be built from this list.

Role plays are restricted to nine prescribed transactional settings (café/restaurant, shop, hotel, train station, tourist info, cinema/theatre, campsite, leisure centre, doctor's surgery, in town). Source: Edexcel 1FR1 Paper 1 Task 2.
Six broad thematic contexts replace earlier topic structures: My personal world, Lifestyle and wellbeing, My neighbourhood, Media and technology, Studying and my future, Travel and tourism.
pedagogical_notes: EEF evidence supports phonics-based instruction in MFL even at secondary level: systematically teaching sound-symbol correspondences in isolation then in cluster words improves transcription and reading-aloud accuracy. Source: educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/education-evidence/teaching-learning-toolkit/phonics.

Retrieval practice is particularly effective for vocabulary retention: short, frequent low-stakes recall beats massed practice. This justifies the Bronze/Silver/Gold practice format with spaced re-exposure. Source: EEF blog 'Why bother with retrieval?', educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk.

NCELP (National Centre for Excellence for Language Pedagogy) recommends a phonics-vocabulary-grammar framework where each item is introduced through its sound, then meaning, then grammatical behaviour. Practice lessons should reflect this by surfacing pronunciation before vocab drilling. Source: ncelp.org/phonics-collection.

Metacognitive strategies (planning what vocab to use, monitoring errors during writing, evaluating after) transfer well to MFL. Worked examples should include a brief 'what I'd check' step to model this. Source: EEF blog 'Metacognition in modern foreign language teaching', educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk.

AI-marked translation and role-play questions should reward communicative success (key message through) over perfect accuracy — exam mark schemes do this. Minor gender or accent errors should not prevent reward if the key idea is communicated.
